theater: 開羅福斯塔斯與尼羅河三角洲

battle.name: 象牙潭之戰
battle.theater: 開羅福斯塔斯與尼羅河三角洲
battle.brief: 909 年初，赫里傑派領袖阿布·海揚自突尼斯方向率軍攻入埃及，圍困開羅與福斯塔斯，三月十八日法蒂瑪王朝的埃及總督穆艾亞德陣亡，城門陷落。埃及月牙劍早在數百年前就退出戰陣，此時只是法蒂瑪王室的儀仗寶物，真正決定城牆攻防的仍是刀劍、長矛、弓弩與攻城器械。

kit.name: 埃及月牙劍
kit.history: 外彎的單刃劍，砍下去不用拔。它比直劍更早出現在埃及人的手上。

countries: 909 年這場發生在尼羅河下游的衝突，表面上是一支北非軍隊攻城，實際捲入三方勢力。其一是法蒂瑪王朝在埃及的統治當局：以開羅與福斯塔斯為都的埃及總督穆艾亞德·希哈卜丁掌軍，哈里發馬赫迪坐鎮北非馬赫迪亞遠程調度，後方還有以巴格達為中心的阿拔斯哈里發朝廷在旁觀望。其二是赫里傑派（又譯伊巴德派殘部）武裝，由突尼斯伊弗里基亞方向南下的首領阿布·海揚·塔米米率領，兵源以柏柏爾系部族民兵為主，輔以伊弗里基亞地方軍與隨軍攻城器械。其三是埃及本地的科普特軍閥與阿拔斯派系游騎，兩面應對，既想借法蒂瑪之力自保，又伺機而動。指揮系統方面，法蒂瑪一方由總督直接統率埃及步兵、馬格里布老兵與象隊，另有從馬赫迪亞出動的艦隊分遣隊負責海上封鎖與糧運；赫里傑派一方以首領個人號令為核心，攻城分三部輪番作業，戰利品按部族分配。史載雙方的軍隊人數、流散部眾與器械數目都沒有留下可信數字，各家編年史多只記勝負、日期與攻城方向。
countriesEn: The clash that unfolded on the lower Nile in 909 looked on the surface like a single North African army besieging a city, but in fact three powers were entangled in it. First was the Fatimid administration in Egypt: the Egyptian governor al-Mu'ayyad Shihab al-Din held command at the joint capital of Cairo and Fustat, while the caliph al-Mahdi sat in Mahdia in North Africa directing the war at long range, with the Abbasid caliphal court at Baghdad watching from the side. Second was the Kharijite (also rendered Ibadi) armed force led by Abu'l-Hayyan al-Tamimi, who came south from Ifriqiya in Tunisia; its manpower was drawn chiefly from Berber tribal militias, supported by Ifriqiyan local troops and siege equipment carried along with them. Third were the local Coptic military strongmen and Abbasid-aligned irregulars in Egypt, who hedged both ways, seeking protection under the Fatimids while waiting for an opportunity. On the command side the Fatimids fielded Egyptian infantry, veteran Maghrebi soldiers and war elephants directly under the governor, plus a naval detachment sent out from Mahdia to enforce the blockade and carry supplies; the Kharijites organised around the personal command of their leader, with three relief turns taking turns at the works and spoils distributed by tribal custom. No reliable figures survive for the size of either army, the numbers of dependents, or the quantity of siege machinery; the chronicles for the most part record only who won, on which dates, and from which direction the attack came.
people: The key figures of this war were fixed into the record only after the fighting, and their names and identities differ between the Arabic, Greek and Chinese versions. The caliph Muhammad al-Mahdi died of illness at Mahdia in North Africa on 17 March 909; on 18 March the Egyptian governor al-Mu'ayyad Shihab al-Din fell in the fighting around besieged Cairo. The two deaths a single day apart form the hinge of the whole episode. The governor's son Abdallah, later known as al-Afdal, succeeded him, but Cairo fell shortly afterwards and he withdrew to North Africa. The besieger Abu'l-Hayyan al-Tamimi was the last Kharijite leader able to move a great army on his own; the accounts say he spent years preparing in Ifriqiya and rallied his followers under the banner of a religious sect, and that after months of siege he entered the city. A year later, in 910, the Fatimid commander Buluggin ibn Ziri sailed north, retook Cairo and took over Egypt; he would eventually found the Zirid dynasty in North Africa, so that his career is the direct reversal of this defeat. Beyond those few names, the commanders of the Ifriqiyan supply fleet and of the Egyptian city garrison survive only in fragmentary notices, and cannot be identified with certainty.

kits: The weapon listed for this battle is the Egyptian khopesh, an outward-curved single-edged bronze chopping sword, a form that predates the straight sword and does not need to be pulled free after a blow. It is an artefact of the fifteenth century before the common era: by 909 it had been extinct as a field weapon for several hundred years and cannot possibly have been used in formed combat. Its place in this conflict therefore lay not on the firing line but in ritual and in the treasury. The Fatimids, sitting in the old pharaonic capital, deliberately borrowed the symbolic vocabulary of Egyptian kingship, and such antiquarian arms became witnesses to royal legitimacy, kept in the palace armoury, carried out with the tents, and displayed in processions and oath ceremonies as objects of grant and honour. The equipment that really decided the assault and the defence was a different set: straight double- or single-edged swords, spears, bows and crossbows, small round and large oval shields, mail and lamellar armour, horses, and counterweight trebuchets, rams, and the tools for digging and filling ditches. Food, drinking water and siege machinery were moved in by camel, mule and donkey trains and by river craft on the Nile, which is why water points and pools became the things actually worth fighting over in a siege.

tactics: The methods used on both sides in this campaign are quite typical for a siege of the period. After crossing into Egypt from North Africa, the Kharijite army did not rush the walls. It first used its cavalry to patrol the roads out of Cairo and cut the city off from reinforcements and from the food resources of the Nile delta and the Alexandrian direction. It then dug a ditch outside the walls and set obstacles there, splitting the besieging force into relief turns that pushed forward with the works and a main body that stood ready, and concentrating the siege engines on a small number of fixed points at the gates and at the ditch. The defenders relied on the continuous walls and towers of Fustat and Cairo, answering with arrows, crossbow bolts, stones from engines, and repeated sorties by mounted troops. The real problem inside the city was not firepower but the rationing of water and grain; the longer the blockade lasted, the more the besiegers themselves depended on seaborne supply. The decisive engagement came at the water features outside the walls: the besiegers sought to control the lines by which water was drawn, hoping to force the garrison into the open, and it was in the collapse of the front and the resulting melee that the gate was carried and the party of Abdallah was driven out. The surviving sources say very little about the course of the engagement at the Ivory Pool, and the ground, the order of battle and the causal chain of the result all remain a matter of conflicting accounts; what is certain is that the besiegers gained Cairo and the defenders paid with the life of their governor.

data: The figures that can be checked are very few, and only those with a basis are set down here. The chronology is the clearest part. The caliph al-Mahdi died at Mahdia on 17 March 909; the Egyptian governor al-Mu'ayyad fell in the siege on 18 March, and Cairo fell in the same stretch of days. The siege itself began in the opening months of 909 and lasted some months before the city was taken, and there is no reliable day-by-day record of the intervening time. As for distance, the run from the Tunisian coast of Ifriqiya to Cairo meant crossing North Africa on land and then moving east along the Mediterranean, or taking the sea route north from Mahdia or Tunis to the neighbourhood of Alexandria in Egypt; by the coastal shipping lanes of the time that also works out to something like eighteen hundred to two thousand kilometres, so that both sides had to keep long lines of supply alive by ship and by pack train. The numbers of troops, of engines and of siege machines are contradictory from source to source; all that can be said is that the besieging host was a coalition in the tens of thousands, drawn from several tribal militias, while the garrison and the city militia numbered from a few thousand to over ten thousand, and that casualties, losses and the value of the plunder in gold, silver, textiles and manuscripts are all beyond reliable reconstruction.

cause: The trigger was the expansion of the Fatimid dynasty in North Africa colliding with the desperate counter-stroke of the Kharijites. Under al-Mahdi the Fatimids treated Ifriqiya and Egypt as two ends of a single theatre of war: one end was territory to be taken, the other was an existing source of taxes and of legitimacy to be held. The Fatimids long tolerated, and even courted, the Ibadi (Kharijite) communities, allowing many Berber clans to convert while keeping their tribal structures, and that population became the pool of men who could be summoned in the late ninth century. Abbasid support, Sunni hostility to Shia government, and the survival of Ibadi polities in the remaining strongholds of the Maghreb, in Tripoli and the western cities, all combined to let Abu'l-Hayyan prepare his expedition well before 909. In Egypt itself the Coptic communities and the local military households had long been dissatisfied with Fatimid taxation and conscription, but they were overawed by the city's defences and by the command of the harbours and did not dare to revolt openly. When Abu'l-Hayyan marched north out of Ifriqiya in the opening months of 909, the siege was itself a probe: to take Cairo and Fustat was to win back the Nile valley's taxes and the Fatimids' legitimacy in the west, and the Abbasid court in Baghdad was only too pleased to see the Fatimids worn down.

impact: The immediate consequence was that the Fatimid hold on Egypt was broken once. The fall and sack of Cairo cost the dynasty the tax stores, the customs posts and the Mediterranean base it had spent years building, while the deaths of the caliph and the governor within a single day created a command vacuum. Abdallah fell back on North Africa, Egypt was thereafter governed from afar, and administrative and military spending had to be squeezed. A year later the Fatimid army returned east under Buluggin ibn Ziri, retook Cairo and restored the shipping and the tolls of the Nile, but the defence of Egypt came henceforth to rest more heavily on Berber troops and fleets transferred from North Africa, and Fatimid control from the centre grew weaker rather than stronger; the politics of Cairo went on turning unstable for years afterwards. From the longer view the war showed that the Ibadi movement still had a capacity for organisation in the Maghreb but none for building a durable state: Abu'l-Hayyan's people could not hold their ground on the Ifriqiyan front, North Africa eventually returned to the Fatimids and then to the Zirid dynasty, and Fatimid rule in Egypt was to last for some decades more before the dynasty was itself replaced late in the tenth century.

result: The outcome has to be read in two stages. As far as March 909 goes, the Kharijites won the visible victory: the Egyptian governor al-Mu'ayyad was killed, Cairo and Fustat were stormed, the royal treasury and much of the wealth of the city were carried off, and the besieging army held Egypt for barely a year before withdrawing back to North Africa. In the longer run the picture is the exact opposite. Already in 910 the Fatimids sent troops east, and a fleet and an army led by Buluggin ibn Ziri retook Cairo, restoring their grip on the shipping and the tolls of the Nile delta; the remaining Kharijite strength in the Maghreb was gradually squeezed, and the fortifications and the civil and religious order of Cairo were rebuilt. As for the engagement itself, the site of the Ivory Pool, the order of battle and the casualty figures are given in conflicting and mutually contradictory ways in the sources. Three points can be held with fair confidence: first, the fighting took place around Cairo in the second and third months of 909 and the siege ended in defeat for the defenders; second, the price the defenders paid was the life of their governor and the sack of the city; third, an antiquarian blade of the khopesh kind appeared here only in the dynasty's regalia and treasury, while the actual course of the war was decided by swords, spears, bows and crossbows, shields and armour, and the engines of the besiegers.
